Rules:
- One commitment per line.
- Write each as a verb phrase: an action followed by its object. For example: "raise the income tax threshold" or "build 300000 new homes".
- State each commitment at the level of a distinct policy action, not its implementation details. Do not subdivide a single commitment into steps.
- Include every commitment. Do not select, rank, prioritise, or judge importance.
- Use the text's own terms for policy objects. Do not substitute synonyms.
- Do not number the lines. No bullets, headings, preamble, or commentary.
- If the text states no policy commitments, output the single word NONE.

# Labour Party Manifesto 2015: Summary

## Core Economic Commitments

The 2015 Labour manifesto centred on a "Budget Responsibility Lock," guaranteeing every policy would be fully funded without additional borrowing. Labour pledged to cut the deficit annually, reduce national debt, and achieve a budget surplus as soon as possible. Key fiscal measures included reinstating the 50p top tax rate for incomes over £150,000, abolishing non-domicile status, and closing tax loopholes. The party committed to maintaining competitive corporation tax rates while cutting and freezing business rates for smaller businesses.

## Work and Living Standards

Labour proposed raising the National Minimum Wage to over £8 per hour by October 2019 and banning exploitative zero-hours contracts. The manifesto promised to promote the Living Wage through government procurement and tax rebates for participating employers. Tuition fees would be reduced from £9,000 to £6,000 annually, and every qualifying school leaver would be guaranteed an apprenticeship. A Compulsory Jobs Guarantee, funded by a bank bonus tax, would provide paid employment for long-term unemployed young people.

## Public Services

The NHS featured prominently, with Labour pledging £2.5 billion more than Conservatives to fund 8,000 additional GPs, 20,000 nurses, and 3,000 midwives, financed through a Mansion Tax on properties exceeding £2 million. The party promised GP appointments within 48 hours, cancer tests within one week, and equal priority for mental and physical health. Labour committed to repealing the Health and Social Care Act, ending NHS privatisation, and integrating physical, mental, and social care services.

Education pledges included protecting the entire education budget, capping class sizes for five-to-seven-year-olds at 30 pupils, requiring qualified teacher status for all state school teachers, and introducing a Technical Baccalaureate for vocational education.

## Families and Housing

Labour promised to expand free childcare from 15 to 25 hours weekly for working parents of three and four-year-olds, double paternity leave to four weeks, and increase paternity pay. The manifesto targeted building 200,000 homes annually by 2020, introducing three-year tenancies with rent rise ceilings, banning unfair letting fees, and abolishing the Bedroom Tax.

## Immigration and Security

The party proposed recruiting 1,000 additional border staff, preventing EU migrants from claiming benefits for two years, and making it illegal to undercut wages through worker exploitation. On security, Labour pledged to protect 10,000 frontline police officers, tackle extremism, and introduce a Violence against Women and Girls Bill.

## Constitutional Reform and Devolution

Major governance reforms included giving 16 and 17-year-olds the vote, replacing the House of Lords with an elected Senate, and passing an English Devolution Act transferring £30 billion to city and county regions. Labour committed to implementing the Smith Agreement for Scotland and establishing fair funding for Wales.

## International Policy

Labour supported continued EU membership while seeking reforms, guaranteed no power transfers to Brussels without a referendum, and committed to NATO membership and the nuclear deterrent. The manifesto emphasised climate change action, maintaining the 0.7% international development commitment, and conducting a Strategic Defence and Security Review.
